detailed_summary.v3.overview: The video proposes a practical, inexpensive muscle-building day for students living in hostels or PG accommodation. Breakfast uses 60 g oats with hot milk, 10–12 almonds, one teaspoon flaxseed, a banana and two boiled eggs. A portable snack combines 100 g roasted chana with a handful of unsalted roasted peanuts. At the hostel mess, the speaker recommends prioritizing salad, roti, dal and curd while limiting oily curries, then adding four egg whites or about 100 g paneer/tofu for extra protein. Pre-workout options include soaked black chana, roasted chana, or a banana-peanut-butter whole-wheat sandwich. Post-workout, the video recommends six egg whites with two bananas, or whey protein in water if affordable. Dinner again uses the mess but adds 100 g paneer. Before bed, it suggests roasted peanuts plus 500 ml low-fat milk. The core value is not a precise bodybuilding prescription but a set of inexpensive substitutions that can upgrade common hostel food toward higher protein and less fried food.

title_en.v1.reason: All twelve foods are clearly named in the transcript.

detailed_summary.v3.overview: The video argues that vegetarian diets can support muscle building when they include adequate protein, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals. It recommends legumes first, especially kidney beans, chickpeas, black chana and lentils, and pairs them conceptually with brown rice to improve amino-acid coverage. Nuts are presented as calorie-dense sources of unsaturated fats and some protein. Milk and curd provide dairy protein and calcium, while fruits supply carbohydrates and micronutrients. Whole wheat is suggested as a staple carbohydrate source. Paneer is positioned as a major vegetarian protein, with homemade lower-fat paneer suggested when saturated fat is a concern. Raw vegetables are included for fiber and micronutrients; sweet potato is proposed as a pre-workout carbohydrate; flaxseed as an omega-3-containing seed; oats as a breakfast or pre-workout staple; and soy chunks as a concentrated protein source. Whey protein receives an honorable mention because it is milk-derived and therefore vegetarian. The food list is useful, but several claims are too absolute: white rice does not need to be categorically eliminated, walnuts are not nutritionally equivalent to fish oil, and moderate soy intake is not well represented by the warning that it causes estrogen-related male breast growth.

Suggested nut serving: about one handful (~28 g).
Milk suggestion: 500–750 ml low-fat milk daily in the source plan.
Paneer serving discussed: 100–200 g daily, with homemade lower-fat paneer as an option.
Sweet potato example: 100 g boiled pre-workout.
limitations: Food needs depend on total calories, protein target, digestion and training goal.
The soy-estrogen warning is overstated relative to typical moderate soy intake.
Walnuts provide ALA omega-3 and are not a direct replacement for EPA/DHA from fish oil.
Brown rice is not universally superior to white rice for muscle gain or fat loss.
